title: Practice: CIA, AAA, and Control Types
objective: By the end of this lesson you can label the CIA pillar harmed in one-line scenarios, match controls to preventive, detective, and corrective types, and decide when a system must fail secure.

blocks.text: You have now read five lessons of definitions, and the exam will hand you none of them as definitions: it hands you one-line stories and expects a label in under a minute. That is a sorting skill, and sorting skills come from reps, not from rereading. This lesson is three short paper drills: label the harm, match the control, spot the fail-secure gap.

For each drill, say your answer out loud before reading the expected result. A wrong answer you hear yourself make is the one you will fix; a wrong answer you only read about fades by tomorrow. Keep every justification to one short sentence: name the harm, the control type, or the failure mode in plain words.
Read each one-line scenario and name the CIA pillar that takes the primary hit: confidentiality, integrity, or availability.

items: S1 — A customer email list is posted to a public forum after a server break-in.
S2 — An attacker quietly changes an order quantity from 1 to 100 before checkout.
S3 — A DNS flood makes the online shop unreachable during a flash sale.
S4 — An auditor finds last month's access logs were rewritten to hide a rogue login.
S5 — A stolen, unencrypted laptop exposes employee medical files.
S6 — A failed firmware update bricks the payment terminals for a full day.
S7 — An on-path attacker swaps the bank account number inside an emailed invoice.
S8 — A crypto-mining infection slows the design workstations to a crawl.

blocks.title: Sort the harm
steps: Label each of S1 to S8 with one CIA pillar: the primary harm, in your own words, in one short sentence.
Mark any scenario where you can argue a second pillar is also harmed, and name it.
For S4 only, decide which single control family would have caught the rewrite: hashing and integrity monitoring, or access control on the logs.
blocks.expected: S1 confidentiality; S2 integrity; S3 availability; S4 integrity (records altered); S5 confidentiality; S6 availability; S7 integrity; S8 availability. Second-pillar arguments: S1 can include availability if the forum posting forces a takedown; S4 can include confidentiality if the rewrite exposed entries; S8 can include integrity if mined data was altered. S4: hashing and integrity monitoring catches rewrites that access control alone may miss, especially by insiders who already have access.

blocks.text: Drill 2: match the control to its type
Each control below does one job first. Label it preventive, detective, or corrective, then add its category: administrative, technical, or physical.

items: C1 — Firewall rules blocking inbound SMB from the internet.
C2 — CCTV cameras at the data center entrance.
C3 — SHA-256 verification of a vendor-supplied file before install.
C4 — Quarterly security awareness training for all staff.
C5 — Restoring encrypted servers from offline backups after ransomware.
C6 — IDS alerting on a known exploit signature.
C7 — Account lockout after ten failed password attempts.
C8 — A lessons-learned meeting that rewrites the password policy after an incident.

blocks.title: Match control to type
steps: For C1 to C8, write the type: preventive, detective, or corrective.
Add the category for each: administrative, technical, or physical.
Pick the one control that would still matter if every preventive control failed, and say why.
blocks.expected: C1 preventive technical; C2 detective physical; C3 detective technical; C4 preventive administrative; C5 corrective technical; C6 detective technical; C7 preventive technical; C8 corrective administrative. The one that still matters: C5 — backups and restore are the last line that brings the business back after prevention and detection both fail. C7 earns debate: it prevents continued guessing but the alert on it feeds detection; grade the primary job first.

blocks.text: When a control loses power or connectivity, it must choose: fail open (keep allowing) or fail secure (keep blocking). Life safety usually wins the argument for doors; security usually wins it for traffic and money.

items: F1 — A hospital ward's electronic door locks lose power; staff and patients must still get through.
F2 — An e-commerce payment-authorization service times out mid-checkout; the site can either let the order through or refuse it.
F3 — A firewall's rule engine crashes; the vendor supports either pass-all or block-all while it restarts.
F4 — A data center's biometric door loses its link to the directory; a leftover script unlocks all doors so staff can keep working.

blocks.title: Spot the fail-secure gap
steps: For F1 to F4, write fail open or fail secure, plus the value that decides it: life safety, revenue, or security.
Name which of the four is a dangerous misconfiguration rather than a defensible choice, and say what should replace it.
Write the one-line rule you would put in policy for door controllers versus network firewalls.
blocks.expected: F1 fail open — life safety beats security on doors; pairs with manned override. F2 fail secure — refuse the order; fraud checks lost means the risk falls on the business, so retry with a clear message. F3 fail secure — block-all; a firewall that passes all while broken is a hole, not a control. F4 the dangerous one: unlocking all doors on a directory outage trades a hard problem for an open building; the fix is fail secure with a guarded physical key override. Policy line: doors fail open only where life safety requires it and never silently; traffic controls fail secure by default.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Read the harm in plain words before touching the answers: seen by the wrong people is C, altered is I, unusable is A. For control questions, name the control's first job: stop it, see it, or fix it. For crash behavior, life safety argues fail open; almost everything else argues fail secure.

blocks.title: Lab: Classify the Controls
blocks.description: Drag ten real controls into preventive, detective, and corrective bins against a graded checklist. Full design: labs/controls-classify.lab.en.md.

cheatsheet: Label the harm in plain words: seen by the wrong people = confidentiality, altered = integrity, unusable = availability.
One event can hit two pillars; the exam wants the primary harm in the story.
Control types by first job: preventive stops it, detective sees it, corrective fixes it; categories are administrative, technical, physical.
Fail-secure default: block traffic and refuse transactions when a control breaks; fail open only for life safety, with a manned override.
Backups and restore are the last line that still matters when prevention and detection both fail.

checkpoint.prompt: After a break-in, an attacker publishes a stolen database of employee medical records on a public website. Which CIA element is harmed MOST?
checkpoint.explanation: The primary harm is exposure: people who should never see the records can now read them. That is confidentiality. The story says nothing about the records being altered or the system going down.

checkpoint.prompt: Which of the following is a detective control?

choices.A: A firewall rule that blocks inbound SMB
choices.B: Requiring dual approval for wire transfers
choices.C: Restoring a server from backup after ransomware
choices.D: Reviewing SIEM logs for anomalous logins

checkpoint.explanation: Log review finds activity that already happened; it sees rather than stops. The firewall rule stops (preventive), the restore fixes (corrective), and dual approval prevents (preventive).

checkpoint.prompt: A firewall's rule engine crashes, and by design all traffic is blocked until the engine restarts. Which behavior does this illustrate?
checkpoint.explanation: When the control breaks, it keeps blocking: that is fail-secure, the safe default for traffic controls. Fail open would pass all traffic through a broken firewall, which turns an outage into an open door.
